name: Motion Capture and Retargeting
title: Motion Capture and Retargeting
answer: Motion capture and retargeting covers the pipeline that turns a performer's movement into a digital skeleton and then maps that skeleton onto a different character, rig, or body. Capture itself ranges from optical marker systems and inertial suits to markerless video pose estimation, and retargeting is the step that makes a jump recorded from one body read correctly on another. In choreography and motion mapping, the field is used to archive dances, previsualise staging, drive game and film characters, and study how movement style survives the transfer between bodies.

sections.body: Motion capture and retargeting covers the pipeline that turns a performer's movement into a digital skeleton and then maps that skeleton onto a different character, rig, or body. Capture itself ranges from optical marker systems and inertial suits to markerless video pose estimation, and retargeting is the step that makes a jump recorded from one body read correctly on another. In choreography and motion mapping, the field is used to archive dances, previsualise staging, drive game and film characters, and study how movement style survives the transfer between bodies.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The stack usually starts with capture hardware or video, then a solver that fits a skeleton to the data, then a retargeting layer that resolves differences in limb length, joint limits, and rest pose. Engines such as Unity and Unreal, and formats such as BVH and FBX, are common places for that skeleton to live, with motion editing tools handling cleanup, looping, and blending. Markerless pipelines lean on pose estimation models, which trade precision for cost and setup time, and the choice between them shapes everything downstream.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners begin with a clean take, then solve and label the skeleton, fix occlusion and foot sliding, and define a source and target rig before retargeting. The hard part is preserving intent: a gesture that reads as weighty on a tall performer can look weightless on a short one, so scale, timing, and contact points are adjusted by hand or by constraint. Retargeting is rarely a single button press, and most work is iteration between the solver, the animation software, and review with the choreographer or director.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions cluster around the performer, the choreographer, and the studio, since a captured body is both personal data and a creative work. Consent and contracts need to cover reuse, re-performance by a digital double, and the training of models on captured motion, and biometric privacy rules can apply to the raw data even when the final animation is not identifiable. Provenance matters too: a take should carry a record of who performed it, when, and under what terms, because retargeted motion is easy to detach from its source. This site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, which shows how live these questions are across creative AI.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Markerless capture keeps improving, which lowers the barrier for small studios and independent choreographers, and generative motion models are beginning to produce or complete movement without a performer. That pushes the field toward hybrid workflows where captured takes seed a model that adapts them to new characters and styles. The open questions are attribution and consent for synthetic motion, and whether retargeting tools will standardise around shared rigs and metadata so that a performance can travel between pipelines without losing its provenance.
